lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun. Wiktionary vowels it with qubuts in the first syllable (כֻּרְכּוּם); everyday spelling כורכום.

profile.feeling: A bright yellow powder: curry, rice, Yemeni spice mixes and “golden” tea.

senses.def: turmeric — the rhizome of Curcuma longa, fresh or (usually) dried and ground, a spice and yellow colouring

examples.tr: Turmeric colours the rice yellow.
At the market I bought a fresh turmeric root.

examples.text: הִיא שׁוֹתָה תֵּה עִם כֻּרְכּוּם וְזַנְגְּבִיל.
examples.tr: She drinks tea with turmeric and ginger.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in Hebrew; the English name turmeric is not used.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology on the Hebrew page. Its Arabic entry كُرْكُم (kurkum, “turmeric”) lists Aramaic כּוּרְכְּמָא (kurkmā) and Hebrew כַּרְכֹּם (karkom) as Semitic cognates, and says the word most likely came via India from Sanskrit कुङ्कुम (kuṅkuma).

funFacts: German Kurkuma, Russian куркума and Greek κουρκουμάς are the same international word as Hebrew כֻּרְכּוּם; Chinese says 姜黄 jiānghuáng, “ginger-yellow” — turmeric is a relative of ginger (זַנְגְּבִיל).
Wiktionary links it to Hebrew כַּרְכֹּם (karkom), the crocus, whose stigmas are saffron: both are “yellow spices”.
pitfalls: Do not confuse it with כַּרְכֹּם (karkom), the crocus or saffron, as in the Song of Songs (4:14): נֵרְדְּ וְכַרְכֹּם “nard and saffron”.
The first u is written with qubuts in vowelled text (כֻּרְכּוּם) but with ו in everyday spelling (כורכום).
subtleties: A mass noun without plural: for one fresh root say שֹׁרֶשׁ כֻּרְכּוּם, for several שָׁרְשֵׁי כֻּרְכּוּם.
Israelis meet it mostly as the yellow powder; the fresh root is sold in health-food shops and markets.

profile.feeling: Sour pink stalks cooked into jams and cakes — a European taste, rare in Israeli shops.

senses.def: rhubarb (Rheum; the sour leaf stalks, cooked like fruit)

examples.tr: Grandma cooks rhubarb jam.

examples.text: אֶת הֶעָלִים שֶׁל הָרִיבָּס לֹא אוֹכְלִים, כִּי הֵם רְעִילִים.
examples.tr: Rhubarb leaves are not eaten, because they are poisonous.
In Germany people love rhubarb cake.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. Compare Arabic رِيبَاس (rībās, “Syrian rhubarb, Rheum ribes”), which Wiktionary derives from Persian ریواس (rivâs), ریباس (ribâs).

funFacts: English rhubarb and German Rhabarber go back, Wiktionary says, to Koine Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν, “foreign rhubarb”; Hebrew רִיבָּס instead matches the Arabic and Persian name.
Botanically a vegetable — you eat the leaf stalk — but it is cooked like a fruit, in jams, compotes and cakes.
pitfalls: Only the stalks are eaten: the leaves contain oxalic acid and are poisonous.
Masculine and used without a plural: רִיבָּס טָרִי; for single stalks say גִּבְעוֹלֵי רִיבָּס.
subtleties: After the article the vowel is qamats, as before every ר: הָרִיבָּס.
רִבָּה “jam” sounds similar but is unrelated: רִבַּת רִיבָּס is a pleasant tongue-twister.

lexemes.note: A loanword used as a mass noun, spelled as in Wiktionary’s English entry wasabi (Hebrew translation ואסאבי, vasabi); other spellings are common. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: The green fire next to the sushi — a sharp jolt up the nose.

senses.def: wasabi — the Japanese root (Wasabia japonica) and the green paste made from it

examples.text: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל סוּשִׁי עִם קְצָת וָאסָאבִּי.
examples.tr: I (m.) eat sushi with a little wasabi.
This wasabi is very hot!

examples.text: רֹב הַוָּאסָאבִּי בַּמִּסְעָדוֹת הוּא בְּעֶצֶם חֲזֶרֶת צְבוּעָה.
examples.tr: Most of the wasabi in restaurants is really dyed horseradish.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the Japanese name is the only one.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From Japanese 山葵 (wasabi), like English wasabi (Wiktionary: “Borrowed from Japanese 山葵 (wasabi)”).

funFacts: Chinese writes it with the same characters as Japanese, 山葵 shānkuí; German and Russian simply borrowed the Japanese name (Wasabi, васаби).
Real wasabi is a relative of cabbage and horseradish, grown in cold mountain streams; it is grated fresh just before eating.
pitfalls: The spelling is not settled: ואסאבי, וסאבי and וואסבי all occur — the pronunciation is always vasabi, with v.
What is sold as wasabi is usually horseradish (חֲזֶרֶת) coloured green; “real wasabi” needs saying.
subtleties: After the article the ו is doubled in vowelled text: הַוָּאסָאבִּי.
The alephs only mark the a vowels (וָאסָאבִּי); they are not pronounced.

lexemes.note: The genus Atriplex (saltbush, orache); used as a mass noun.

profile.feeling: A grey, salty desert shrub — and the famine food of the Book of Job.

senses.def: saltbush, orache — plants of the genus Atriplex with edible, spinach-like leaves (garden orache: Atriplex hortensis)

examples.text: אֶת הֶעָלִים שֶׁל הַמַּלּוּחַ אֶפְשָׁר לְבַשֵּׁל כְּמוֹ תֶּרֶד.
examples.tr: The leaves of orache can be cooked like spinach.
Saltbush shrubs grow in the desert.
who pick saltbush among the shrubs (Job 30:4)

phrases.tr: who pick saltbush among the shrubs
phrases.meaning: said of starving outcasts who live on wild plants

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym: the plant is not a market vegetable, and the botanical genus name is the only word.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): compare Arabic مُلَّاح (mullāḥ, “seepweed”). The word belongs to the root מ־ל־ח of מֶלַח “salt”, like the adjective מָלוּחַ “salty”: saltbushes grow on salty soils and taste salty.

funFacts: German calls garden orache Gartenmelde and Russian лебеда; in Russian history лебеда was famine food — exactly as מַלּוּחַ is in the Book of Job.
The Mediterranean saltbush, Atriplex halimus, grows wild on Israel’s coast and in its deserts; its leaves really do taste salty.
pitfalls: מַלּוּחַ (the plant, with a doubled ל) and מָלוּחַ (“salty”) are both spelled מלוח and both pronounced malúakh — only the vowel marks and the context tell them apart.
subtleties: Garden orache is barely known in Israel; to most speakers מַלּוּחַ is the wild desert saltbush.
In the Bible (Job 30:4) the outcasts “pick saltbush among the shrubs” — a picture of hunger.

ref.src: Composed from the Wiktionary (kaikki.org) entries לֵב (plural לְבָבוֹת) and דֶּקֶל; Wiktionary’s English entry heart of palm gives לב דקל (lev dékel, masculine)

profile.feeling: Pale, tender cylinders from a can — a salad treat.

senses.def: heart of palm — the tender inner core of certain palms, eaten as a vegetable

examples.tr: I opened a can of hearts of palm for the salad.

examples.text: הִיא חוֹתֶכֶת אֶת לִבְבוֹת הַדֶּקֶל לְעִגּוּלִים.
examples.tr: She cuts the hearts of palm into rounds.

examples.text: לֵב דֶּקֶל טָרִי הוּא מַעֲדָן נָדִיר.
examples.tr: A fresh heart of palm is a rare delicacy.

collocations.tr: a can of hearts of palm

etymology.text: לֵב “heart” (Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *libb-; also “heart, core, center”) + דֶּקֶל “palm tree” (Wiktionary: first attested in Mishnaic Hebrew, of uncertain origin; cognate with Aramaic דִּקְלָא) — like English heart of palm and German Palmherz.

funFacts: Hebrew לֵב is cognate with Arabic لُبّ (lubb, “core, kernel”) and Aramaic לִבָּא (Wiktionary) — the “heart” of a palm is its core in every sense.
Cutting the heart used to kill the palm; today much of it comes from multi-stemmed palms such as the peach palm, which grow new shoots.
pitfalls: The plural of לֵב is לְבָבוֹת, in a construct לִבְבוֹת: לִבְבוֹת דֶּקֶל, not *לֵבִים.
The article goes on the second word: לֵב הַדֶּקֶל, לִבְבוֹת הַדֶּקֶל.
subtleties: דֶּקֶל alone is a palm tree (and in Wiktionary also its date); the vegetable needs the whole phrase.
In everyday talk the plural is the normal form, as on the can: לִבְבוֹת דֶּקֶל.

profile.feeling: A summer weed of fields and roadsides — and a leafy green in Indian, Greek and Arab kitchens.

senses.def: amaranth — plants of the genus Amaranthus; their leaves eaten as greens
amaranth seed, eaten like a grain

examples.tr: Amaranth grows in the fields in summer.
In Indian cooking amaranth leaves are cooked.

examples.text: אֶת זַרְעֵי הַיַּרְבּוּז אוֹכְלִים כְּמוֹ דָּגָן.
examples.tr: Amaranth seeds are eaten like a grain.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry and no etymology. English amaranth comes (via French and Latin) from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “unfading”), with the ending influenced by ἄνθος “flower” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In Greece the boiled greens are βλίτα, a classic summer salad with olive oil and lemon; Chinese 苋菜 xiàncài is the same leafy vegetable.
The Greek name ἀμάραντος, “unfading”, comes from the flowers, which keep their colour when dried.
pitfalls: To most Israelis יַרְבּוּז is a weed, not food; when you mean the vegetable say עֲלֵי יַרְבּוּז.
subtleties: After the article the י is doubled: הַיַּרְבּוּז.

profile.feeling: A pale root in the bunch of soup vegetables — the smell of Friday chicken soup.

senses.def: root parsley, Hamburg parsley (the root of Petroselinum crispum var. tuberosum)

examples.text: סַבְתָּא שָׂמָה שֹׁרֶשׁ פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה בִּמְרַק הָעוֹף.
examples.tr: Grandma puts a parsley root in the chicken soup.

examples.text: בַּשּׁוּק מוֹכְרִים שָׁרְשֵׁי פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה לְיַד הַגְּזָרִים.
examples.tr: At the market they sell parsley roots next to the carrots.
The parsley root looks like a parsnip.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה alone means the leaves.

etymology.text: שֹׁרֶשׁ “root” (from Proto-Semitic *šurš-) + פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה “parsley” (Wiktionary: from European languages, from Latin petroselinum, itself from Greek πετροσέλινον, “rock celery”).

funFacts: German Petersilienwurzel is the same “parsley root”; Russian петрушка and German Petersilie come from the same Greek πετροσέλινον, while Modern Greek and Turkish say μαϊντανός / maydanoz.
Root parsley and leaf parsley are one species: one variety is bred for its root, the other for its leaves.
pitfalls: פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה alone is the leafy herb; the root vegetable needs שֹׁרֶשׁ.
The plural changes the first word: שָׁרְשֵׁי פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה (said shorshei, spelled שורשי).
subtleties: It is easily taken for a parsnip (גֶּזֶר לָבָן); the parsley root is slimmer and tastes of parsley.
In שָׁרְשֵׁי the first vowel is a qamats katan, pronounced o.
